rows.text: Source A is a poster by the national water agency. It was put up at bus stops, and it is about the price of water going up from 1 July.

Source A wants to say that the rise in the price of water is needed and is small. It says 'Every drop costs more to make', and that for most families the rise is 'less than the price of one cup of coffee a week'.

Source A wants to say that the rise in the price of water is needed and is small. It says 'Every drop costs more to make', and that for most families the rise is 'less than the price of one cup of coffee a week'. It is speaking to households, the families who pay the water bill. It talks about 'most families' and promises rebates 'for smaller flats'.

Source A wants to say that the rise in the price of water is needed and is small. It says 'Every drop costs more to make', and that for most families the rise is 'less than the price of one cup of coffee a week'. It is speaking to households, the families who pay the water bill. It talks about 'most families' and promises rebates 'for smaller flats'. The poster was put up in the month before the first rise, when many people were unhappy about paying more. The agency wants households to accept the rise calmly and to start saving water before it comes. That is why it tells them 'Use a little less, and you may pay no more than before'.
Source B is an interview with the owner of a noodle stall and Source C is a letter from a mother. Both are about the rise in the price of water.
They are similar in showing that the rise means people pay more. B says 'My bill will go up by about $60 a month'. C says 'my family pays about $3 more a month'.

They are similar in showing that the rise means people pay more. B says 'My bill will go up by about $60 a month'. C says 'my family pays about $3 more a month'. They are different on whether people can use less water. B says 'I cannot use less water' because 'A clean stall needs water'. C says 'My children now take shorter showers', so the family did cut its use.

B is bitter and wants readers to see the rise as unfair to small stalls, so the owner ends with 'It is small for an office, not for me'. C is fair and wants the help to be explained better, so the letter grants 'That I can manage' but warns that 'Nobody told her about the rebate in a language she reads'.
Source E is useful because it is a report by university researchers and it is about the price of water.
Source E is useful. It shows that the higher price did make households save water: 'Households used 4% less water per person in the first six months'. So the rise did what it was meant to do.

Source E is useful. It shows that the higher price did make households save water: 'Households used 4% less water per person in the first six months'. So the rise did what it was meant to do. It can be trusted. The researchers do not work for the water agency, they 'studied the water bills of 800 households', and they report the good and the bad: use fell, yet 'the fall was uneven'. Source D supports the figure. The spokesperson also says households 'used 4% less water per person'. Source C supports the finding on small flats: a family in a two-room flat says 'My children now take shorter showers'. It is limited in one way. It tells us how much water was saved, not why the money was needed. So it is very useful for showing who saved water and what it cost them, and less useful for judging whether the agency had to raise the price.
Source D is reliable because it is from a ministry spokesperson. The ministry is in charge of water, so it knows what happened.

Source D is reliable. It says 'households used 4% less water per person' and 'That is the biggest drop in ten years'. These are clear facts and figures, so it shows that the rise was the right decision.

Source D is not fully reliable. It says 'The rise has worked' because 'households used 4% less water per person'. Source E gives the same figure, so that part is true. But E says 'the fall was uneven': large flats and houses 'cut their use by 1%' while one-room and two-room flats 'cut by 9%'. D also says rebates 'covered most of the rise', yet E found that in the smallest flats one in five now 'flush or wash less often than they think is healthy'. The check shows that D is right about the total but leaves out who did the saving and what it cost them. So it cannot be fully trusted as evidence that the decision was right.

The speaker wants them to accept the rise, so the speech picks the best figures and ends with 'our children'. That purpose makes it weak evidence that the decision was right. Only the fall in water use can be trusted, because the researchers found the same figure.
I agree because water is precious and people waste it. If water costs more, people will be more careful with it.

The sources that agree are weaker. D is the ministry defending its own decision, and F is a group that campaigns to save water and looks only at the waste. E is by researchers with no side to defend. It gives the same fall as D, but shows that large flats and houses 'cut their use by 1%' while the smallest flats 'cut by 9%'. So the rise changed least the homes that use the most. Source C is balanced. The writer was 'angry' at first, then found the family 'pays about $3 more a month' and saves water. Yet the same letter tells of a neighbour who is 'afraid of the bill'. So I agree only to a small extent: a higher price does save water, but it was not right to lean on price alone when it presses hardest on small flats and stalls.

I agree. The Treaty of Versailles was signed in 1919. Germany had to pay reparations of 6.6 billion pounds. Germany also lost land and its army was cut to 100 000 men. There was a War Guilt Clause too. The Germans called it a diktat. So Germans hated the Treaty for many reasons.

I agree to a large extent. Reparations were an important reason. In 1919 the Treaty did not name a sum, so Germans faced an unknown bill. Only in 1921 was the amount fixed, at 132 billion gold marks, about 6.6 billion pounds. Germans felt this was impossible for a country already worn out by four years of war. Germany was already printing money and prices were rising. When it failed to keep up its payments, French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr, its main industrial area, in January 1923. The government printed even more money to pay the workers there who stopped work, and inflation became hyperinflation. The savings of ordinary families became worthless. Germans blamed the reparations for this suffering. This shows reparations made Germans hate the Treaty more and more as the cost became real, because it brought hardship into their own homes. The War Guilt Clause also made Germans angry.

Germans felt this was impossible for a country already worn out by four years of war. Germany was already printing money and prices were rising. When it failed to keep up its payments, French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr, its main industrial area, in January 1923. The government printed even more money to pay the workers there who stopped work, and inflation became hyperinflation. The savings of ordinary families became worthless. Germans blamed the reparations for this suffering. This shows reparations made Germans hate the Treaty more and more as the cost became real, because it brought hardship into their own homes.

However, the War Guilt Clause also made Germans hate the Treaty. Article 231 made Germany accept responsibility for the loss and damage of the war. Most Germans read this as being blamed for starting the war. They believed they had fought to defend their country and that other countries shared the blame. A proud nation felt it had been branded a criminal in front of the world. Separately, Germany was not allowed to take part in the talks at Paris and was simply told to sign, so Germans called the Treaty a diktat, a dictated peace. This shows that the War Guilt Clause made Germans hate the Treaty because it humiliated them.

So both reparations and the War Guilt Clause were reasons why Germans hated the Treaty of Versailles.

I agree only to a small extent that reparations were the main reason. The War Guilt Clause came first: it was because Germany had to accept responsibility that the Allies could demand payment for the damage. So Germans who hated the reparations were also hating the clause behind them. The clause also hurt every German from the day the Treaty was signed in June 1919, while the sum for reparations was not even fixed until 1921, and the worst pain came in 1923 and eased after the Dawes Plan of 1924 made the payments easier. So the War Guilt Clause was the main reason, because reparations rested on it and its insult lasted longer.

I agree. The Treaty of Versailles was signed in 1919 and Germans hated it. There was the Kapp Putsch in 1920 and the French went into the Ruhr in 1923. There was hyperinflation and money became worthless. The Weimar Republic also had proportional representation and many parties. So the Weimar Republic was unstable for many reasons.

I agree to a large extent. The Treaty of Versailles was an important reason. The Weimar politicians signed it in June 1919. Many Germans already called them the November Criminals for ending the war in 1918, and now blamed them for the harsh terms as well. The Treaty cut the army to 100 000 men, and in March 1920 angry Freikorps soldiers who were to be disbanded seized Berlin in the Kapp Putsch. Germany was already printing money and prices were rising. When it fell behind with the Treaty's reparations, French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr in January 1923. The government printed even more money to pay the workers who stopped work, and inflation became hyperinflation, which wiped out people's savings. This shows the Treaty made the Republic unstable because it turned Germans against their own government and brought one crisis after another. The Weimar constitution was also a problem.

The Treaty of Versailles was an important reason. The Weimar politicians signed it in June 1919. Many Germans already called them the November Criminals for ending the war in 1918, and now blamed them for the harsh terms as well. The Treaty cut the army to 100 000 men, and in March 1920 angry Freikorps soldiers who were to be disbanded seized Berlin in the Kapp Putsch. Germany was already printing money and prices were rising. When it fell behind with the Treaty's reparations, French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr in January 1923. The government printed even more money to pay the workers who stopped work, and inflation became hyperinflation, which wiped out people's savings. This shows the Treaty made the Republic unstable because it turned Germans against their own government and brought one crisis after another.

However, the Weimar constitution also made the Republic unstable. It used proportional representation, so many small parties won seats in the Reichstag and no single party had a majority. Every government was a coalition of parties that disagreed with each other, and coalitions often broke up. There were about eight Chancellors between 1919 and 1923. Such short-lived governments could not take firm decisions in a crisis, and President Ebert had to use emergency powers under Article 48 many times to rule by decree. Germans saw that their new democracy did not work well and gave it little loyalty. This shows the constitution made the Republic unstable because it produced weak governments.

So both the Treaty of Versailles and the Weimar constitution were reasons why the Republic was unstable.

I agree to a large extent that the Treaty was the main reason. The constitution stayed the same after 1923, yet in the years 1924 to 1929, when Stresemann was the leading figure, the Republic was much more stable, with no putsch and a recovering economy. This suggests that coalition government could work when there was no crisis. Not every crisis came from the Treaty: the Spartacist rising of January 1919 came before it. But between 1919 and 1923 it was the Treaty that supplied most of the crises: the anger at the terms, the Kapp Putsch and the Ruhr occupation. The constitution only made the government slow to deal with them. So the Treaty was the main reason, because it created most of the problems that the weak governments then failed to solve.

I agree. Korea was divided at the 38th parallel in 1945. Kim Il Sung was the leader of North Korea and Syngman Rhee was the leader of South Korea. Kim Il Sung wanted to rule all of Korea. On 25 June 1950 North Korea invaded South Korea. The Soviet Union and China were communist countries too. So this is how the Korean War started.

I agree to a large extent. Kim Il Sung's wish to rule all of Korea was an important reason. Korea had been divided at the 38th parallel in 1945, and in 1948 two separate states were set up: communist North Korea under Kim Il Sung and non-communist South Korea under Syngman Rhee. Each leader claimed to be the rightful ruler of the whole country. Kim was determined to unite Korea under communist rule by force. He built up his army and went to Moscow in 1949 and again in 1950 to ask Stalin to approve an invasion. On 25 June 1950 North Korean forces crossed the 38th parallel, and they captured Seoul within days. This shows that the war began because Kim wanted the whole of Korea and planned and launched the attack to get it. The Soviet Union also supported North Korea, which was another reason.

Kim Il Sung's wish to rule all of Korea was an important reason. Korea had been divided at the 38th parallel in 1945, and in 1948 two separate states were set up: communist North Korea under Kim Il Sung and non-communist South Korea under Syngman Rhee. Each leader claimed to be the rightful ruler of the whole country. Kim was determined to unite Korea under communist rule by force. He built up his army and went to Moscow in 1949 and again in 1950 to ask Stalin to approve an invasion. On 25 June 1950 North Korean forces crossed the 38th parallel, and they captured Seoul within days. This shows that the war began because Kim wanted the whole of Korea and planned and launched the attack to get it.

However, the support and signals of the outside powers also led to the war. Stalin refused Kim's request in 1949, but agreed in 1950. By then the Soviet Union had tested its own atomic bomb in August 1949, and the communists had won power in China in October 1949. Stalin made his approval depend on Mao agreeing, which Mao did in May 1950. The Soviet Union gave North Korea tanks, heavy guns, planes and military advisers. The USA also seemed unlikely to fight. American troops had left South Korea in 1949, and in January 1950 the American Secretary of State, Dean Acheson, gave a speech that left South Korea outside the line the USA promised to defend in the Pacific. This shows that the outside powers gave Kim the weapons and the confidence to invade, so the war broke out.

So both Kim Il Sung's wish to rule all of Korea and the support and signals of the outside powers were reasons for the outbreak of the Korean War.

I agree only to some extent that Kim's wish to rule all of Korea was the main reason. Kim's aim did not change: he wanted the same thing in 1949 as in 1950, and Syngman Rhee in the south also wanted to rule the whole country. Yet there was no war in 1949, because Stalin said no. What changed in 1950 was the support of the Soviet Union, the agreement of China and the belief that the USA would stay out. North Korea could not invade without Soviet tanks and Stalin's approval. So the support and signals of the outside powers mattered more, because they turned Kim's wish into a war that could actually be fought.

I agree. China entered the Korean War in October 1950 when the United Nations forces were near the Yalu River. Many Chinese soldiers fought in Korea. General MacArthur was dismissed by President Truman in 1951. There were peace talks for two years. The armistice was signed on 27 July 1953 at Panmunjom. So the war ended in a stalemate.

I agree to a large extent. China's entry into the war was an important reason. In September 1950 United Nations forces led by the American general MacArthur landed at Inchon and drove the North Koreans back. In October 1950 they crossed the 38th parallel, captured Pyongyang and moved towards the Yalu River, the border with China. It looked as if the United Nations would win and unite Korea. China feared having American troops on its border, so from October 1950 it sent hundreds of thousands of soldiers into Korea. They pushed the United Nations forces back below the 38th parallel and took Seoul in January 1951. The United Nations forces retook Seoul in March 1951, and the fighting then settled near the 38th parallel. This shows that China's entry cancelled out the United Nations advance, so neither side could defeat the other. President Truman also wanted to keep the war small, which was another reason.

China's entry into the war was an important reason. In September 1950 United Nations forces led by the American general MacArthur landed at Inchon and drove the North Koreans back. In October 1950 they crossed the 38th parallel, captured Pyongyang and moved towards the Yalu River, the border with China. It looked as if the United Nations would win and unite Korea. China feared having American troops on its border, so from October 1950 it sent hundreds of thousands of soldiers into Korea. They pushed the United Nations forces back below the 38th parallel and took Seoul in January 1951. The United Nations forces retook Seoul in March 1951, and the fighting then settled near the 38th parallel. This shows that China's entry cancelled out the United Nations advance, so neither side could defeat the other.

However, the wish of both sides to keep the war limited also led to a stalemate. MacArthur wanted to bomb China and widen the war. President Truman refused, because he feared a larger war with China and with the Soviet Union, which had had the atomic bomb since 1949. He dismissed MacArthur in April 1951. On the communist side, the Soviet Union did not send its army into the war, and China sent its soldiers as volunteers and did not declare war on the USA. Peace talks began in July 1951 but dragged on for two years, mainly over the return of prisoners of war. After Eisenhower became President in January 1953 and Stalin died in March 1953, both sides were ready to stop. An armistice was signed at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953, with the border close to the 38th parallel. This shows that because neither side would use its full strength, neither could win.

So both China's entry into the war and the wish of both sides to keep the war limited were reasons why the Korean War ended in a stalemate.

I agree to a large extent that China's entry was the main reason. In October 1950 the United Nations forces were close to winning the whole of Korea, so without China there would have been a victory, not a stalemate. China's entry is what made the two sides evenly matched on the battlefield. The decision to keep the war limited came afterwards and because of it: Truman had to choose between a wider war with China and a draw, and he chose the draw. So China's entry mattered more, because it created the stalemate, while the limits on the war only explain why it was not broken.
A sustainable neighbourhood is one that is good for the future, so the government should build more of them.
Recycling bins can be placed at the foot of every block.
Recycling bins can be placed at the foot of every block. Rainwater can also be collected from the roofs and used again.

Recycling bins can be placed at the foot of every block. Residents put their paper, cans and plastic bottles there to be recycled, so less rubbish has to be burnt. Rainwater can also be collected from the roofs and used again.

Recycling bins can be placed at the foot of every block. Residents put their paper, cans and plastic bottles there to be recycled, so less rubbish has to be burnt. Rainwater can also be collected from the roofs and used again. It can be used for washing the void decks, so less treated tap water is needed.
Fires are very dangerous hazards and a resilient neighbourhood is one that is strong when fires happen.
Residents can go for courses to pick up emergency skills.
Residents can go for courses to pick up emergency skills. They can also make the effort to know the people living around them.

Residents can go for courses to pick up emergency skills. They learn how to use a fire extinguisher and do first aid, so they can start helping before the fire engine comes. They can also make the effort to know the people living around them.

They can also make the effort to know the people living around them. Then when something happens they will check on each other, like helping an old neighbour who lives alone to get out.

Elderly people walk slowly and their eyesight is weaker, so roads are more dangerous for them than for younger people.
The green man at the traffic light can stay on longer so that old people who walk slowly have enough time to get across.

A small island can be built in the middle of the road so that old people can cross half the road, rest, and then cross the other half.
A tropical cyclone is a very big storm with strong winds and heavy rain. It is also called a typhoon or a hurricane.
The sea is very warm, at least 26.5 °C, so a lot of water evaporates and the air above it is warm and wet.
The sea is very warm, at least 26.5 °C, so a lot of water evaporates and the air above it is warm and wet. This warm, wet air goes up and leaves low pressure near the sea surface.

The sea is very warm, at least 26.5 °C, so a lot of water evaporates and the air above it is warm and wet. This warm, wet air goes up and leaves low pressure near the sea surface. As it goes up it cools and the water vapour condenses into huge clouds, which gives out heat.

The sea is very warm, at least 26.5 °C, so a lot of water evaporates and the air above it is warm and wet. This warm, wet air goes up and leaves low pressure near the sea surface. As it goes up it cools and the water vapour condenses into huge clouds, which gives out heat. Air from all around rushes in towards the low pressure, and this makes strong winds.
Tropical cyclones are very dangerous, and many places near warm seas get them every year.
The very strong winds cause damage.
The very strong winds cause damage. They can rip the roofs off houses and pull trees out of the ground.

The city can build sea walls along its coast.
